**Trump orders regulators to ease fintech access to US payment rails**

*An executive order directing federal agencies to review rules governing fintech participation in payment systems signals a deregulatory push that could reshape competitive dynamics for European firms operating in the US.*

President Trump signed an executive order on May 19 directing federal financial regulators to review regulations, guidance, supervisory practices and application processes that affect how fintechs interact with banks and payment infrastructure. The order covers access to payment rails, bank-fintech partnerships and licensing frameworks across the broader financial services sector.

The practical effect will depend on how individual agencies respond, but the direction of travel is clear: the administration wants to lower barriers for non-bank payment providers. For European fintechs and payment firms with US operations or ambitions, this could open new avenues for direct participation in clearing and settlement systems. It also sharpens the contrast with Europe's approach, where PSD3 and the payment services regulation are tightening supervisory requirements for payment institutions rather than loosening them.

The order arrives as debate continues over the CFPB's open banking rule, which remains paused by a court order. Taken together, the moves suggest the US is pursuing market access for fintechs through executive action rather than the data-sharing frameworks that have defined European open banking policy.

*Sources: [White House Pushes FinTech Access to Payment Rails](https://www.pymnts.com/news/regulation/2026/white-house-pushes-fintech-access-to-payment-rails/) — PYMNTS*

**NMI acquires Dwolla to build out account-to-account payments stack**

*The deal combines NMI's white-label payment acceptance platform with Dwolla's account-to-account and open banking capabilities, creating a combined operation processing nearly $700 billion and signalling continued consolidation in embedded payments infrastructure.*

NMI, a private equity-backed embedded payments firm, has acquired Dwolla, an API-first platform specialising in account-to-account payments, real-time money movement and open banking connectivity. Dwolla serves more than 400 clients. The financial terms were not disclosed.

The acquisition follows a pattern now well established in payments infrastructure: platform companies buying specialist account-to-account capabilities to offer merchants and software partners alternatives to card rails. NMI's pitch is a single white-label platform spanning card acceptance, account-to-account transfers and payment orchestration. The deal sits alongside NAB's acquisition of Banked last week as evidence that acquirers see pay-by-bank infrastructure as a necessary layer rather than a standalone business.

For European observers, the consolidation underscores the gap between account-to-account payments as a technology, which is maturing rapidly, and account-to-account payments as a consumer-facing product, which still lacks the ubiquity and dispute resolution frameworks that cards provide. The acquirers are betting that embedding account-to-account into broader platforms is the path to scale.

*Sources: [NMI Acquires Dwolla to Strengthen Pay by Bank Offering](https://www.pymnts.com/acquisitions/2026/nmi-acquires-dwolla-to-strengthen-a2a-payment-offerings/) — PYMNTS | [NMI acquires Dwolla](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47780/nmi-acquires-dwolla) — Finextra | [NMI's Latest Deal Snags A2A Platform Dwolla](https://www.digitaltransactions.net/nmis-latest-deal-snags-a2a-platform-dwolla/) — Digital Transactions*

stories.original:
**Monzo's fraud reimbursement costs surge 85% under PSR mandatory rules**

*The digital bank's sharp increase in authorised push payment fraud payouts offers the first clear evidence of how the PSR's reimbursement regime is hitting challenger banks disproportionately.*

Monzo has reported an 85% increase in fraud reimbursement payouts, driven by the Payment Systems Regulator's mandatory reimbursement framework for authorised push payment fraud introduced in October 2024. The regime requires sending payment service providers to reimburse victims up to £85,000 within five business days, with costs shared between sending and receiving firms.

The scale of the increase matters because it quantifies a cost pressure that the industry has discussed in theoretical terms. Challenger banks such as Monzo, which serve younger and more digitally active customer bases, may face higher claim volumes relative to their revenue than traditional high street banks. The figures will likely intensify calls from some quarters to revisit the £85,000 cap or adjust the cost-sharing mechanism.

The data also feeds into the broader question of where fraud liability should sit. The PSR's framework places it squarely on payment firms, but industry voices, such as those from telecoms and social media platforms, are increasingly being drawn into the debate about upstream responsibility for enabling fraud.

*Sources: [Monzo's fraud payouts soar 85% under UK reimbursement rules](https://www.thebanker.com/content/7028b289-e103-4757-adfa-04007b699e51) — The Banker*

stories.original:
**UK regulators publish tenth regulatory initiatives grid with PSR merger in view**

*The latest cross-regulator grid maps upcoming UK financial services initiatives through 2028, giving firms a consolidated view of the regulatory pipeline as the PSR's planned absorption into the FCA approaches.*

The Bank of England, FCA, PSR, PRA and the Pensions Regulator have published the tenth edition of the Regulatory Initiatives Grid, setting out planned consultations, policy statements and rule changes across financial services. The grid is designed to help firms plan for regulatory change by presenting a single timeline of forthcoming initiatives.

For payments firms, the grid arrives at a moment of structural uncertainty. The UK Financial Services Bill, currently making its way through Parliament, will fold the PSR into the FCA. The grid therefore captures a regulatory landscape that is itself about to be reorganised. Firms will want to track which PSR initiatives, such as the APP fraud reimbursement review and ongoing work on interchange and card scheme fees, will carry over intact and which may be reshaped under the FCA's broader mandate.

The Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland, responding to the grid, cautioned against treating regulation purely as a barrier to growth, noting that businesses are unlikely to see substantive effects from many of the listed initiatives before 2028. That timeline reinforces the point that regulatory planning in UK payments now requires a multi-year horizon.

*Sources: [Tenth edition of the Regulatory Initiatives Grid](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/report/2026/tenth-edition-of-the-regulatory-initiatives-grid) — Bank of England | [ICAS warns against viewing regulation as barrier to growth](https://www.theaccountant-online.com/news/icas-warns-against-viewing-regulation/) — The Accountant Online | [Latest edition of the Regulatory Initiatives Grid published](https://www.regulationtomorrow.com/2026/05/latest-edition-of-the-regulatory-initiatives-grid-published-3/) — Global Regulation Tomorrow*
